title: Al-Wajid, the Finder
tomorrow: the hand that gives, or the hand that gets: which is honored?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Qayyum: the One on the night shift, holding it all up. The line: he holds it up. And a question about three verses that all begin the same way.
screen: `HE HOLDS IT UP.` → `DID HE NOT FIND THEE?`

segments.voice: Everyone's at the beach this week. The stories roll past: a sunset, matching sunglasses, a group photo with one face missing, and the face is yours. Missing out has its own ache, and a phone can make it hourly. Surah ad-Duha speaks to someone in a low season, and it asks three questions, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)? Did He not find thee wandering and direct (thee)? Did He not find thee destitute and enrich (thee)?"
screen: `THE BEACH, WITHOUT YOU.` → `MISSING OUT, HOURLY.` → `DID HE NOT FIND THEE?`

segments.voice: The verses speak to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and tradition says they came in a season when he felt left behind. Find, in those questions, is the Arabic wajada, and it shares its root with today's Name: Al-Wajid, the Finder. It's a Name from the traditional list rather than a word the Qur'an itself uses as a Name. It means the one for whom nothing is out of reach, and so the one who lacks nothing. The surah doesn't say the hard season wasn't real. It counts what was found anyway: protection, direction, enough. And enrich how? A hadith answers that the way a friend might: richness isn't having lots of things; real richness is richness of the soul. So lacking nothing isn't having everything, or being at every beach. It's knowing what you've already been handed. Then the surah does something worth telling a friend tonight. It doesn't end on the person being comforted. It turns outward: don't crush the orphan, don't turn away the one who asks, and speak of your Lord's blessings. The one who was found becomes a finder.
screen: `FIND: WAJADA, THE FINDER'S ROOT.` · `PROTECTION, DIRECTION, ENOUGH.` · `RICHNESS OF THE SOUL.` · `THE FOUND BECOME FINDERS.` · then, large: `LACKING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Look around wherever you are and find three things you already have that you once hoped for: a key to a door, a coat, a person who would pick up if you called. Rest your attention on each one for a few breaths. Then, for the rest of the two minutes, sit with the sentence: right now, nothing I truly need is missing.
screen: `THREE THINGS YOU ONCE HOPED FOR.` · `NOTHING I TRULY NEED IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Al-Wajid. The Finder: the one for whom nothing is out of reach, who lacks nothing and leaves the found rich in soul.
Words to carry: lacking nothing, the way the found are rich. That's day fifteen thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims recite Surah ad-Duha in prayer and in hard seasons, and the hadith 'richness is richness of the soul' is quoted when speaking of contentment.

fork.setup: your friend didn't get into the program everyone else in your group got into. she says, 'i have nothing now.' what fits Surah ad-Duha?
options: tell her the program wasn't worth it anyway.
say the miss is real, name what's still found in her life, and stay close.
tell her to stop comparing, since feelings aren't facts.
fork.reveal: ad-Duha doesn't pretend the low season isn't real. it counts what was found anyway, then turns outward to the one who asks. staying close is that turn.

original.note: Arabic: the Finder, who lacks nothing; from the traditional list, sharing a root with wajada, to find, in Surah ad-Duha.

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a lost-and-found desk.
what it means: nothing is out of His reach, so He lacks nothing, and those He finds are made rich in soul.
what a scholar hears: wajada in 93:6–8; al-Wajid in the Tirmidhi list, not a Qur'anic name form; 'richness is richness of the soul' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6446).
